<!-- slide 4 -->
# Stacked Bar Plots {.divider}

[Composition · proportions]{.eyebrow}


<!-- slide 5 -->
## What Is a Stacked Bar? {.smaller}

[Stacked bar · theory]{.eyebrow}

### Every column sums to the whole; bands stack to show its parts

A **stacked bar** answers one question: *what is each sample made of?* Each column is a single observation (an individual, a tumour, a microbiome sample). The bar is sliced into coloured **bands**, one per category, and the heights of those bands sum to the total. When every bar has the same total — say, a proportion that must add to 100% — the chart becomes a pure **composition** view.

**Use it when**:

- **Admixture / ancestry**: each individual = one bar made of ancestry fractions K1…K5.
- **Microbiome**: each sample = one bar of phylum or genus relative abundance.
- **Cell-type deconvolution**: each tumour = one bar of immune-cell fractions.

**Avoid it when** only the totals matter (a plain bar chart is clearer) or when you need to *compare a single inner band across many samples* (segment baselines wobble — a line, dot plot, or small multiples wins).


<!-- slide 6 -->
## Anatomy, Before Any Data {.smaller}

[Stacked bar · theory]{.eyebrow}

### Four bars, five bands — how the geometry works

Before touching real ancestry data, build the **idea**. Four cartoon bars, each made of five rectangles in the course palette. The trick is the `bottom=` argument: each band starts where the previous one ended.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 4.4

# CREATE — a tiny empty canvas for the anatomy cartoon
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.4))

# four fake samples, each a 5-component composition that sums to 1.0
samples = ["A", "B", "C", "D"]
comp = np.array([
    [0.55, 0.20, 0.10, 0.10, 0.05],   # sample A
    [0.30, 0.35, 0.20, 0.10, 0.05],   # sample B
    [0.10, 0.20, 0.40, 0.20, 0.10],   # sample C
    [0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.35, 0.30],   # sample D
])
band_names = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]

# stack bands one at a time, tracking the running "bottom" for each bar
bottom = np.zeros(len(samples))                       # start every bar at y = 0
for k in range(5):                                     # one band per K component
    ax.bar(samples, comp[:, k], bottom=bottom,        # CALL: draw this band atop the last
           color=COURSE_PAL[k], edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.6,
           label=band_names[k])
    bottom += comp[:, k]                              # next band starts where this one ended

# cosmetic frame
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylabel("composition")
ax.set_xlabel("sample")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5), frameon=False, fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide 7 -->
## Stacked Bar · The Data {.smaller}

[Stacked bar · data peek]{.eyebrow}

### One row per individual — population label + five ancestry fractions

`load_admixture()` returns 120 individuals across five reference populations (EUR / EAS / AFR / AMR / SAS). Each row carries five ancestry components **K1…K5** whose values sum to 1.0 — they are mixture proportions, the output of a tool like ADMIXTURE or STRUCTURE.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column

adm = load_admixture()           # individual, population, K1..K5 (K1..K5 sum to 1)
adm.head(5)
```


<!-- slide 8 -->
## Stacked Bar · Step 1 — One Individual {.smaller}

[Stacked bar · build]{.eyebrow}

### 1 · A single bar, K1…K5 stacked on top of each other

Build the **idea** on one person. Take row 0 (an EUR individual), stack their five K fractions vertically with `ax.bar(..., bottom=running_total)`. The bar height ends at exactly 1.0 because the proportions sum.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-2|4-6|8-9|11-16|18-20"}
adm = load_admixture()                          # the full ancestry table
row = adm.iloc[0]                                # one individual (the first EUR)

# the five mixture proportions for this person
k_cols = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]          # column names in order
fracs  = [row[k] for k in k_cols]                # numeric values, sum to 1.0

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.8, 4.6))       # CREATE the canvas
bottom = 0                                        # start the stack at y = 0

for i, k in enumerate(k_cols):                    # one band per K component
    ax.bar(row["individual"], fracs[i],          # CALL: draw this band
           bottom=bottom,                         # stack it atop the previous
           color=COURSE_PAL[i], edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.6,
           label=k)
    bottom += fracs[i]                            # next band starts here

ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.set_ylabel("ancestry fraction")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5), frameon=False, fontsize=9)
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}

#| fig-width: 3.8
#| fig-height: 4.6
```

<!-- slide 9 -->
## Stacked Bar · Step 2 — One Population, Sorted {.smaller}

[Stacked bar · build]{.eyebrow}

### 2 · All EUR individuals, sorted by their K1 contribution

Now scale to every EUR individual. Sort them by **K1** so the dominant ancestry forms a smooth gradient — without sorting, the bars look like noise. The `for` loop is unavoidable here: matplotlib's `ax.bar` needs the running `bottom` updated per band.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-4|6-7|9-10|12-19|21-23"}
adm = load_admixture()                                       # full table
k_cols = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]

eur = adm[adm["population"] == "EUR"].copy()                 # one population
eur = eur.sort_values("K1", ascending=False)                 # gradient by K1

x = np.arange(len(eur))                                       # 0, 1, 2, ... one slot per ind
bottom = np.zeros(len(eur))                                   # running total per bar

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 4.2))                    # CREATE the canvas

for i, k in enumerate(k_cols):                                # one band across all bars
    heights = eur[k].values                                   # bracket access — safe
    ax.bar(x, heights, bottom=bottom,                         # CALL: draw the band
           color=COURSE_PAL[i], width=1.0,                    # width=1.0: bars touch
           edgecolor="none", label=k)
    bottom += heights                                          # advance the stack

ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(eur) - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_ylabel("ancestry fraction")
ax.set_title("EUR individuals — sorted by K1", color=MUTED, fontsize=11)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5), frameon=False, fontsize=9)
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}

<!-- slide 10 -->
## Stacked Bar · Step 3 — Every Population {.smaller}

[Stacked bar · build]{.eyebrow}

### 3 · All five populations, separators between groups

The canonical admixture plot. Sort *within* each population by its dominant K, concatenate, then draw thin vertical lines between groups so the eye can find the boundaries.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-4|6-11|13-14|16-23|25-30"}
adm = load_admixture()                                            # full table
k_cols = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]
pops = ["EUR", "EAS", "AFR", "AMR", "SAS"]                        # fixed order
dom  = {"EUR": "K1", "EAS": "K2", "AFR": "K3", "AMR": "K4", "SAS": "K5"}

# sort each population internally by its dominant K, then concatenate
ordered = pd.concat([
    adm[adm["population"] == p]                                    # one population
       .sort_values(dom[p], ascending=False)                       # gradient inside
    for p in pops
], ignore_index=True)

x = np.arange(len(ordered))                                        # slot per individual
bottom = np.zeros(len(ordered))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.0, 4.2))                         # CREATE the canvas

for i, k in enumerate(k_cols):                                     # paint each band
    heights = ordered[k].values
    ax.bar(x, heights, bottom=bottom,                              # CALL
           color=COURSE_PAL[i], width=1.0, edgecolor="none", label=k)
    bottom += heights

# population boundaries: vertical hairlines
counts = ordered["population"].value_counts().reindex(pops)        # how many per pop
boundaries = counts.cumsum().values[:-1]                            # cut points
for b in boundaries:
    ax.axvline(b - 0.5, color=CREAM, lw=1.5)                       # thin cream divider

ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(ordered) - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_ylabel("ancestry fraction")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}

<!-- slide 11 -->
## Stacked Bar · Step 4 — Labels & Legend {.smaller}

[Stacked bar · build]{.eyebrow}

### 4 · Population names along the x, K legend on the right

The composition is right; now make it readable. Centre each population's name *under its block* of bars using the cumulative counts, and pin the K legend outside the axes so it never overlaps the data.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="25-32|34-38"}
adm = load_admixture()
k_cols = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]
pops = ["EUR", "EAS", "AFR", "AMR", "SAS"]
dom  = {"EUR": "K1", "EAS": "K2", "AFR": "K3", "AMR": "K4", "SAS": "K5"}

ordered = pd.concat([
    adm[adm["population"] == p].sort_values(dom[p], ascending=False)
    for p in pops
], ignore_index=True)

x = np.arange(len(ordered))
bottom = np.zeros(len(ordered))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.0, 4.4))

for i, k in enumerate(k_cols):
    heights = ordered[k].values
    ax.bar(x, heights, bottom=bottom,
           color=COURSE_PAL[i], width=1.0, edgecolor="none", label=k)
    bottom += heights

counts = ordered["population"].value_counts().reindex(pops)
boundaries = counts.cumsum().values[:-1]
for b in boundaries:
    ax.axvline(b - 0.5, color=CREAM, lw=1.5)

# population labels: place each at the middle of its block
edges  = np.concatenate([[0], counts.cumsum().values])               # block edges
mids   = (edges[:-1] + edges[1:]) / 2                                # midpoints
ax.set_xticks(mids)                                                   # tick at each mid
ax.set_xticklabels(pops, color=MUTED, fontsize=10)                    # population names
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=0)                                    # hide tick marks

ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(ordered) - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylabel("ancestry fraction")
ax.set_title("ADMIXTURE K=5 — 120 individuals across 5 populations", color=INK)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(title="component", loc="center left",
          bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5), frameon=False, fontsize=9)
```
:::

<!-- slide 12 -->
## Stacked Bar · Pandas Variant {.smaller}

[Stacked bar · ergonomic]{.eyebrow}

### Three lines with `pandas.DataFrame.plot(stacked=True)`

Pandas wraps matplotlib for the common case. Set the population-ordered index on the K columns and ask for a stacked bar — pandas computes the running `bottom=` for you. You give up control (no per-population sort across groups, harder custom separators), but you get to a publishable draft in three lines.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-3|5-8|10-13"}
adm = load_admixture()
k_cols = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]
pops = ["EUR", "EAS", "AFR", "AMR", "SAS"]

# group-ordered frame: each pop sorted by its dominant K, indexed by individual
ordered = pd.concat([adm[adm["population"] == p].sort_values(k_cols[i], ascending=False)
                     for i, p in enumerate(pops)], ignore_index=True)
data = ordered.set_index("individual")[k_cols]                # rows=ind, cols=K1..K5

# CALL: pandas builds the whole stacked bar from the frame
ax = data.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, width=1.0,
               color=COURSE_PAL, figsize=(9.0, 4.0), legend=True)
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.set_ylabel("ancestry fraction")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5), frameon=False, fontsize=9)
```

**Trade-off**: pandas wins on conciseness; matplotlib wins on **control** — custom separators, per-population sort orders, labels at block midpoints. Use pandas to **draft**, matplotlib to **publish**.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9.0
#| fig-height: 4.0

adm = load_admixture()
k_cols = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]
pops = ["EUR", "EAS", "AFR", "AMR", "SAS"]

ordered = pd.concat([adm[adm["population"] == p].sort_values(k_cols[i], ascending=False)
                     for i, p in enumerate(pops)], ignore_index=True)
data = ordered.set_index("individual")[k_cols]

ax = data.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, width=1.0,
               color=COURSE_PAL, figsize=(9.0, 4.0), legend=True)
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.set_ylabel("ancestry fraction")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5), frameon=False, fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 13 -->
## Stacked Bar · Takeaway {.smaller}

[Stacked bar · recap]{.eyebrow}

### Composition first, totals only if they vary

::: {.takeaway}
[The recipe]{.tl}
1. **Each column is one observation**; bands stack to its total.
2. **Sort within groups** by the dominant component — un-sorted admixture looks like noise.
3. **One colour per band, fixed across bars** — the eye tracks a band by its colour.
4. **Separators between groups** (thin cream lines) replace heavy x-ticks.

When the totals are forced equal (admixture proportions sum to 1), the stacked bar is **pure composition**. When totals vary (read counts, dollars), it shows **composition *and* magnitude** in one chart. Pick deliberately.
:::
